The exact blossom matching takes the two outer edges A–B and C–D, in the accent color with their endpoints, for a total weight of 4 + 4 = 8; the heavier middle edge B–C is faded. The card notes that the greedy method would lock in B–C first and stop at a total of 5." width="100%"} A matching is a set of edges with no shared endpoints, so each node is paired with at most one partner. The maximum-weight matching is the matching whose edges have the largest possible total weight. It answers questions such as "which pairs of workers and tasks, players and teams, or donors and recipients give the best total compatibility, if everyone joins at most one pair?". On an unweighted graph every edge counts as `1`, so the result is a maximum matching: as many pairs as possible. With `maxcardinality=True`, the matching first uses as many edges as possible and only then maximizes the weight, so it may take a light edge if that lets one more pair form. Edges with zero or negative weight are only ever chosen in that mode. The default `method="blossom"` is exact. `method="greedy"` instead takes edges from heaviest to lightest whenever both endpoints are still free; it is faster on very large graphs but only guaranteed to reach half of the optimal weight. Edge direction is ignored, self-loops are never chosen, and among parallel edges only the heaviest can be chosen. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [maxcardinality]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, return a maximum-weight matching among the matchings with the most edges. Default `False`. [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to use edge weights. If `None` (default), follows the graph's `weighted` flag; with `False` every edge counts as `1`. [method]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["blossom"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : `"blossom"` (default, exact) or `"greedy"` (fast half-approximation; ignores `maxcardinality=`). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The IDs of the matched edges, in ascending order. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `method=` is unknown or an edge weight is not finite. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Edmonds' algorithm (1965) grows alternating trees from the unmatched nodes and keeps a feasible solution of the linear-programming dual: one variable per node and one per *blossom*, an odd cycle of tight edges that is shrunk into a single node. When no tight edge extends the search, the duals are adjusted until a new edge becomes tight, a blossom is expanded, or (without `maxcardinality=`) a node's dual drops to zero. Each augmentation enlarges the matching by one edge, giving $O(V^3)$ time overall. This is a port of Joris van Rantwijk's implementation, which NetworkX also uses, and the total weight always matches NetworkX's (when there are several optimal matchings, the one returned may differ). The greedy method sorts the edges in $O(E \log E)$ and is a $\tfrac{1}{2}$-approximation (Preis, 1999). ## Examples {.doc-examples} In this path the heaviest edge B-C is a trap: taking it blocks both A-B and C-D, which together weigh more. The exact matching takes the outer pair: ::: {#dc97070f .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(weighted=True).add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) g.add_edges([("A", "B", 4.0), ("B", "C", 5.0), ("C", "D", 4.0)]) exact = g.maximum_weight_matching() greedy = g.maximum_weight_matching(method="greedy") def total(ids): return sum(g.get_edge(e).weight for e in ids) # Returns (8.0, 5.0): the greedy method locks in B-C total(exact), total(greedy) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (8.0, 5.0) ``` ::: ::: With `maxcardinality=True`, the matching must use as many edges as possible, even if that lowers the total weight. Here the heavy edge A-B alone (weight 10) beats the two light edges A-C and B-D (total 2), but only the light pair matches every node: ::: {#1a42e3f7 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(weighted=True).add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) g.add_edges([("A", "B", 10.0), ("A", "C", 1.0), ("B", "D", 1.0)]) [ [g.get_edge(e).weight for e in g.maximum_weight_matching(maxcardinality=mc)] for mc in (False, True) ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [[10.0], [1.0, 1.0]] ``` ::: ::: On an unweighted graph, the result is a maximum matching. A 4 x 4 grid has a perfect matching of 8 edges: ::: {#5508d50e .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} grid = ec.Graph().add_grid_2d(4, 4) matching = grid.maximum_weight_matching() len(matching), grid.is_perfect_matching(matching) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (8, True) ``` ::: :::
